title: Real Numbers
notes: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (FTA): Every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique apart from the order of factors.

To find HCF and LCM by prime factorisation: write each number as a product of prime powers. HCF = product of the SMALLEST power of each common prime. LCM = product of the GREATEST power of each prime that appears in any of the numbers.
Important relation (only for TWO numbers): HCF(a, b) x LCM(a, b) = a x b. This does NOT hold for three or more numbers.
Theorem 1.2: If p is a prime number and p divides a^2, then p divides a (a is a positive integer). This is the key tool used to prove irrationality.

Proof by contradiction is the standard technique to prove a number is irrational: assume it IS rational (= p/q, q not 0, p and q coprime), then derive a contradiction (usually that p and q share a common factor after all).
Standard irrational proofs to know cold: root2, root3, root5, and combinations like 5 - root3, 3*root2, 7*root5 (sum/difference/product of a nonzero rational and an irrational is always irrational).
For three numbers p, q, r the FTA-based HCF/LCM shortcut does not directly apply; use the special formulas given in the chapter's 'Note to the Reader' if three-number LCM/HCF is asked.

formulas.name: Euclid's Division Lemma
formulas.formula: a = bq + r, where 0 <= r < b
formulas.use: Basis of the division algorithm; used to find HCF via repeated division.

formulas.name: HCF x LCM relation (2 numbers)
formulas.formula: HCF(a,b) x LCM(a,b) = a x b
formulas.use: Find one of HCF/LCM when the other and the product are known.

formulas.name: HCF by prime factorisation
formulas.formula: Product of smallest powers of common primes
formulas.use: Fast HCF for numbers already factorised.

formulas.name: LCM by prime factorisation
formulas.formula: Product of greatest powers of all primes present
formulas.use: Fast LCM for numbers already factorised.

formulas.name: LCM of three numbers
formulas.use: Special case, three numbers only (see Note to Reader).

formulas.name: HCF of three numbers
formulas.use: Special case, three numbers only (see Note to Reader).

examples.question: Consider 4^n where n is a natural number. Check whether there is any value of n for which 4^n ends with digit zero.
examples.solution: 4^n = (2)^(2n), so its only prime factor is 2. For a number to end in 0 it must have 5 as a factor too (since 10 = 2x5). By uniqueness in FTA, 4^n can never have 5 as a factor. So no value of n makes 4^n end in 0.

examples.question: Find the LCM and HCF of 6 and 20 by prime factorisation.
examples.solution: 6 = 2^1 x 3^1, 20 = 2^2 x 5^1. HCF = 2^1 = 2 (smallest common power). LCM = 2^2 x 3^1 x 5^1 = 60 (greatest powers of all primes present).

examples.question: Find HCF of 96 and 404 by prime factorisation, hence find LCM.
Find HCF and LCM of 6, 72 and 120 using prime factorisation.
examples.solution: 6 = 2x3, 72 = 2^3x3^2, 120 = 2^3x3x5. HCF = 2^1x3^1 = 6. LCM = 2^3x3^2x5^1 = 360. Note: product of the three numbers is NOT equal to HCF x LCM here -- that shortcut only works for two numbers.

examples.question: Prove that root3 is irrational.
examples.solution: Assume root3 = a/b in lowest terms (a, b coprime, b not 0). Squaring: 3b^2 = a^2, so a^2 is divisible by 3, hence a is divisible by 3 (Theorem 1.2). Write a = 3c. Substituting: 3b^2 = 9c^2, so b^2 = 3c^2, meaning b is also divisible by 3. Now both a and b share factor 3, contradicting that they were coprime. So root3 is irrational.

examples.question: Show that 5 - root3 is irrational.
examples.solution: Assume 5 - root3 = a/b (rational). Rearranging gives root3 = 5 - a/b = (5b-a)/b, a ratio of integers, meaning root3 would be rational -- contradiction, since root3 is irrational. Hence 5 - root3 is irrational.

examples.question: Show that 3*root2 is irrational.
examples.solution: Assume 3*root2 = a/b (rational, coprime a,b). Then root2 = a/(3b), a ratio of integers, so root2 would be rational -- contradiction. Hence 3*root2 is irrational.

exercises.answer: (i) LCM=182, HCF=13 (ii) LCM=23460, HCF=2 (iii) LCM=3024, HCF=6

exercises.question: Find LCM and HCF by prime factorisation: (i) 12, 15, 21 (ii) 17, 23, 29 (iii) 8, 9, 25
exercises.answer: (i) LCM=420, HCF=3 (ii) LCM=11339, HCF=1 (iii) LCM=1800, HCF=1

exercises.question: Check whether 6^n can end with digit 0 for any natural number n.
exercises.answer: No -- 6^n = 2^n x 3^n has no factor of 5, so it can never end in 0.

exercises.question: Explain why 7x11x13+13 and 7x6x5x4x3x2x1+5 are composite numbers.
exercises.answer: Both expressions have a common factor (13 and 5 respectively) greater than 1 and less than the number itself, so both are composite.

exercises.question: Sonia takes 18 minutes and Ravi takes 12 minutes for one round of a circular field, starting together in the same direction. After how many minutes will they meet again at the start?
Prove that root5 is irrational.
exercises.answer: Proof by contradiction using Theorem 1.2, same structure as root2/root3 proof.

exercises.question: Prove that 3 + 2*root5 is irrational.
exercises.answer: Assuming it is rational leads to root5 being expressible as a ratio of integers, contradicting that root5 is irrational.

exercises.question: Prove that the following are irrational: (i) 1/root2 (ii) 7*root5 (iii) 6+root2
exercises.answer: Each reduces to assuming root2 or root5 is rational via algebraic rearrangement, contradicting their known irrationality.
